records.source: וַיְמַ֤ן יְהוָה֙ דָּ֣ג גָּד֔וֹל לִבְלֹ֖עַ אֶת־יוֹנָ֑ה וַיְהִ֤י יוֹנָה֙ בִּמְעֵ֣י הַדָּ֔ג שְׁלֹשָׁ֥ה יָמִ֖ים וּשְׁלֹשָׁ֥ה לֵילֽוֹת׃
records.gloss: And Yahweh appointed a fish great to swallow Jonah, and Jonah was in [the] belly of the fish three days and three nights.
pieces: But {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} appointed a great fish to swallow Jonah, and Jonah was inside the fish for three days and three nights.

L.1: And {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} appointed a great fish to swallow Jonah, and Jonah was in the inner parts of the fish three days and three nights.

R.1: But {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} sent a huge fish to swallow Jonah. And Jonah was inside the fish for three days and three nights.

decisions.choice: This verse is 2:1 in the Hebrew text, 1:17 in Bibles that follow the Latin and later numbering
decisions.reason: The Hebrew text begins chapter 2 with the fish, so that the chapter holds the whole episode inside it. Many Bibles end chapter 1 with this verse, numbering it 1:17, so their 2:1-10 is 2:2-11 here. Open Word Bible follows the numbering of the Hebrew text it translates, and Jonah is cited by the Hebrew numbers.

decisions.choice: a great fish: a huge sea creature, not named more closely
decisions.reason: The Hebrew word is the ordinary word for fish, and "great" is the book's word for everything that is more than ordinary (see 1:2). The text does not say what kind of creature it was; Hebrew did not class sea creatures as modern zoology does. The traditional "whale" comes from later retellings and from reading the Greek word of Matthew 12:40, not from the Hebrew.

decisions.choice: three days and three nights in the fish: the sign of Jonah in Matthew 12:40
decisions.reason: Jesus says: "Just as Jonah was in the belly of the sea monster three days and three nights, so the Son of Man will be in the heart of the earth three days and three nights" (Matthew 12:40; compare Luke 11:29-30). Matthew's Greek word means a large sea creature; it is the word the Greek translation uses here. The Hebrew says "a great fish".

decisions.choice: appointed: assigned a task by God
decisions.reason: The verb means to count out or assign. The same verb is used for the plant, the worm and the east wind that God appoints in chapter 4 (4:6, 7, 8). The fish is God's servant, sent to save Jonah from drowning, and it obeys him (2:11) as Jonah did not.

decisions.choice: a great fish (L, B); a huge fish (R), never "whale"; appointed (L, B); sent (R); in the inner parts of (L); inside (B, R)
decisions.reason: As set for Jonah, the creature is "a great fish" at Literal and Balanced and "a huge fish" at Readable, as Matthew 12:40 has at that level. "Appointed" stays the same word each time God appoints something (m4); Readable says "sent" each time.

records.heading: The great fish and Jonah's prayer

records.source: וַיִּתְפַּלֵּ֣ל יוֹנָ֔ה אֶל־יְהוָ֖ה אֱלֹהָ֑יו מִמְּעֵ֖י הַדָּגָֽה׃
records.gloss: And prayed Jonah to Yahweh his God from [the] belly of the fish.
pieces: Then Jonah prayed to {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} his God from inside the fish.

L.2: And Jonah prayed to {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} his God from the inner parts of the fish.

R.2: From inside the fish, Jonah prayed to {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} his God.

decisions.choice: This verse is 2:2 in the Hebrew text, 2:1 in Bibles that follow the Latin and later numbering
decisions.reason: Because the Hebrew text begins chapter 2 one verse earlier (see the note at 2:1), Hebrew 2:2-11 is 2:1-10 in many Bibles. Open Word Bible follows the Hebrew numbering.

decisions.choice: Jonah prayed from the belly of the fish: the psalm that follows thanks God for rescue from drowning
alternatives: a prayer for rescue from the fish
decisions.reason: The prayer in verses 3-10 is a psalm of thanksgiving: it looks back on sinking into the sea, calling to God and being heard, and ends with a promise of sacrifice. The fish is the rescue. Jonah gives thanks from inside it, before he reaches dry land. The psalm is full of phrases from the Psalms, noted verse by verse.

decisions.choice: the fish: the same fish, with a different ending
decisions.reason: Here the Hebrew word for fish has a feminine ending; in 2:1 and 2:11 it does not. Both forms are used for fish in general (Genesis 1:26; Exodus 7:18), and the same creature is meant.

decisions.choice: Jonah prays: his first prayer in the book
decisions.reason: The sailors prayed while Jonah slept (1:5-6, 14). Here, at last, he prays, and calls the LORD "his God".

records.source: וַיֹּ֗אמֶר קָ֠רָאתִי מִצָּ֥רָה לִ֛י אֶל־יְהוָ֖ה וַֽיַּעֲנֵ֑נִי מִבֶּ֧טֶן שְׁא֛וֹל שִׁוַּ֖עְתִּי שָׁמַ֥עְתָּ קוֹלִֽי׃
records.gloss: And he said: I called from distress of mine to Yahweh, and he answered me; from [the] belly of Sheol I cried for help; you heard my voice.
pieces: He said: \q "When I was in trouble I cried out to {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}, and {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} gave me an answer; \q from deep in Sheol I called for help, and {{deity_pronoun:you|You}} heard my voice.

L.3: And he said: \q "I called out of my distress to {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}, and {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} answered me; \q out of the belly of Sheol I cried for help; {{deity_pronoun:you|You}} heard my voice.

R.3: He said: \q "When I was in trouble, I called to {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}. And {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} answered me. \q From deep in the grave I cried for help, and {{deity_pronoun:you|You}} heard me.

decisions.choice: I called in my distress to the LORD, and he answered me: as Psalm 120:1 and 18:7
decisions.reason: Psalm 120:1 says "To the LORD in my distress I called, and he answered me", and Psalm 18:7 "In my distress I called on the LORD ... he heard my voice". Jonah prays in the words of Israel's psalms. The wording follows Psalm 120:1 where the Hebrew is the same; Jonah's order of words differs.

decisions.choice: the belly of Sheol: the depths of death
decisions.reason: Sheol is the place of the dead (Psalm 18:6). To be in its "belly" is to be as good as dead, swallowed by death as Jonah was swallowed by the fish (2:1). Jonah speaks of drowning as going down to the dead, as the psalms do of mortal danger (Psalm 30:4; 88:4-7).

decisions.choice: he answered me ... you heard: the psalm speaks of God and then to him
decisions.reason: The first line tells others what the LORD did; the second turns to address him. Such changes of person are common in the psalms of thanksgiving (Psalm 30:2-4; 116).

decisions.choice: the psalm, verses 3-10, is set as poetry; the story around it is prose
decisions.reason: The words of Jonah's prayer are poetry, in balanced lines, and are set in lines. The verses that tell the story before and after it (2:1-2, 11) are prose, as chapters 1, 3 and 4 are.

decisions.choice: When I was in trouble I cried out to the LORD, and he gave me an answer (B); Sheol (L, B); the grave (R)
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable reuse the wording of Psalm 120:1 at their levels (m1). Literal follows Jonah's own order of words. Readable says "the grave" for Sheol, as set for the prophets. Jonah's words are quoted speech in a narrative, so they take double quotation marks, which close at the end of verse 10; "And he said" stands on its own line before the psalm, as in 2 Samuel 22:2.

records.source: וַתַּשְׁלִיכֵ֤נִי מְצוּלָה֙ בִּלְבַ֣ב יַמִּ֔ים וְנָהָ֖ר יְסֹבְבֵ֑נִי כָּל־מִשְׁבָּרֶ֥יךָ וְגַלֶּ֖יךָ עָלַ֥י עָבָֽרוּ׃
records.gloss: And you cast me [into the] deep, into [the] heart of [the] seas, and a river surrounded me; all your breakers and your waves over me passed.
pieces: You threw me into the depths, into the heart of the seas, \q and the current swirled around me; \q all {{deity_pronoun:your|Your}} breaking waves and rollers have gone over my head.

L.4: You cast me into the deep, in the heart of the seas, \q and a river surrounded me; \q all {{deity_pronoun:your|Your}} breakers and {{deity_pronoun:your|Your}} waves have passed over me.

R.4: You threw me deep into the sea. \q The water swirled all around me. \q All {{deity_pronoun:your|Your}} waves crashed over me.

decisions.choice: you cast me: Jonah sees God's hand behind the sailors' act
decisions.reason: The sailors threw Jonah overboard (1:15), but he says that God did it. The storm was the LORD's, and so was the throw; Jonah knows that his punishment came from God. The verb here is not the one used in chapter 1 for hurling, but a common word for casting or throwing.

decisions.choice: all your breakers and your waves have passed over me: the words of Psalm 42:8
decisions.reason: The last line is the same, word for word, as the second half of Psalm 42:8. The waves are God's, because he rules the sea (1:9).

decisions.choice: the current: the river of the deep
decisions.reason: The word usually means a river. Here it is the streams or currents of the deep sea, perhaps with a hint of the waters thought to flow beneath the world (Psalm 24:2, where the same word is used of the sea's "rivers").

decisions.choice: cast (L); threw (B, R); a river (L); the current (B); the water (R); breakers ... waves (L); breaking waves and rollers (B)
decisions.reason: Literal and Balanced reuse the wording of Psalm 42:8 at their levels for the last line. Readable shortens it to "all your waves", as it uses plain words for the sea throughout. "You" begins a sentence at each level, so it takes no setting span there.

records.source: וַאֲנִ֣י אָמַ֔רְתִּי נִגְרַ֖שְׁתִּי מִנֶּ֣גֶד עֵינֶ֑יךָ אַ֚ךְ אוֹסִ֣יף לְהַבִּ֔יט אֶל־הֵיכַ֖ל קָדְשֶֽׁךָ׃
records.gloss: And I said, I have been driven away from before your eyes; yet I will again look to [the] temple of your holiness.
pieces: I said, 'I have been driven away from {{deity_pronoun:your|Your}} sight; \q still, I will look again toward {{deity_pronoun:your|Your}} holy temple.'

L.5: And I said, 'I have been driven out from before {{deity_pronoun:your|Your}} eyes; \q yet I will look again toward {{deity_pronoun:your|Your}} holy temple.'

R.5: I said, 'You have thrown me out of {{deity_pronoun:your|Your}} sight. \q But I will look again toward {{deity_pronoun:your|Your}} holy temple.'

decisions.choice: driven out from before your eyes: as Psalm 31:23
decisions.reason: Psalm 31:23 says "I said in my alarm, 'I am cut off from before your eyes'". Jonah, who fled "from the presence of the LORD" (1:3), now fears that he has been driven from it for good. The verb is the one used of Adam and Eve driven out of the garden (Genesis 3:24) and of Cain (Genesis 4:14).

decisions.choice: yet I will look again: Jonah's hope even when cast out
alternatives: how will I look again toward your holy temple?
decisions.reason: The Hebrew word here means "yet" or "surely": though driven out, Jonah will look to the temple again. By a change of one letter it would be "how", making the line a cry of despair, "How will I ever look again toward your holy temple?" One of the later Greek translations, Theodotion's, is said to read it that way. The Hebrew text is followed. This description of the Greek is written from general knowledge.

decisions.choice: look toward your holy temple: turn in prayer to the place where God is present
decisions.reason: Solomon asked God to hear those who pray toward the temple from far away (1 Kings 8:38, 44, 48), and the psalms speak of looking to the temple in prayer (Psalm 5:8; 138:2). The temple may be the one in Jerusalem or God's dwelling in heaven; in verse 8 the prayer reaches it.

decisions.choice: driven out from before your eyes (L); driven away from your sight (B); You have thrown me out of your sight (R)
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable say "sight" for "before your eyes". Readable makes the passive active, naming God, which is what Jonah means (verse 4). The words Jonah said to himself take single quotation marks, because they stand inside his prayer.

records.source: אֲפָפ֤וּנִי מַ֨יִם֙ עַד־נֶ֔פֶשׁ תְּה֖וֹם יְסֹבְבֵ֑נִי ס֖וּף חָב֥וּשׁ לְרֹאשִֽׁי׃
records.gloss: They encompassed me, waters, up to [the] neck; [the] deep surrounded me; reeds [were] wrapped around my head.
pieces: The waters closed over me up to my throat; \q the deep was all around me; \q seaweed was wrapped around my head.

L.6: The waters closed in on me up to [my] neck; \q the deep surrounded me; \q reeds were wrapped around my head.

R.6: The water was up to my neck. \q The deep sea was all around me. \q Seaweed was wrapped around my head.

decisions.choice: up to the neck: up to the throat, at the point of death
alternatives: to the point of taking my life
decisions.reason: The word often translated "soul" or "life" also means the throat or neck (Psalm 69:2, where the same phrase is used of water rising to the neck). The water reached his throat and threatened his life; both senses are present.

decisions.choice: the waters up to the neck: as Psalm 69:2
decisions.reason: Psalm 69:2 says "Save me, God, for the waters have come up to my neck". Jonah uses the same picture of drowning.

decisions.choice: the deep ... reeds: the ocean depths and the weeds of the sea
decisions.reason: "The deep" is the great ocean (Genesis 1:2; Psalm 42:8). The word for "reeds" is the one in the name of the Red Sea, the "Sea of Reeds"; here it is the weed of the sea floor, wound around Jonah's head as he sank.

decisions.choice: up to [my] neck (L); up to my throat (B); up to my neck (R); reeds (L); seaweed (B, R)
decisions.reason: Each level reuses the wording of Psalm 69:2 at that level for "up to the neck" (m2). Balanced and Readable say "seaweed" for the reeds of the sea.

records.source: לְקִצְבֵ֤י הָרִים֙ יָרַ֔דְתִּי הָאָ֛רֶץ בְּרִחֶ֥יהָ בַעֲדִ֖י לְעוֹלָ֑ם וַתַּ֧עַל מִשַּׁ֛חַת חַיַּ֖י יְהוָ֥ה אֱלֹהָֽי׃
records.gloss: To [the] roots of [the] mountains I went down; the earth, its bars [were] around me forever; and you brought up from [the] pit my life, Yahweh my God.
pieces: I went down to the roots of the mountains; \q the earth's bars closed behind me forever. \q But {{deity_pronoun:you|You}} brought my life up from the pit, {{divine_name:LORD|Yahweh}} my God.

L.7: To the roots of the mountains I went down; \q the earth with its bars [was] around me forever; \q but {{deity_pronoun:you|You}} brought up my life from the pit, {{divine_name:LORD|Yahweh}} my God.

R.7: I sank down to where the mountains begin. \q The land of the dead locked me in forever. \q But {{deity_pronoun:you|You}} brought me up alive from the grave, {{divine_name:LORD|Yahweh}} my God.

decisions.choice: the roots of the mountains: the bottom of the sea, where the mountains were thought to stand
decisions.reason: The mountains were pictured as resting on foundations deep under the earth and the sea (Psalm 18:8; Job 28:9). Jonah sank as far down as anyone could go. His descent from Joppa (1:3) ends here.

decisions.choice: the earth with its bars: the land of the dead, pictured as a city with barred gates
alternatives: the dry land shut him out, its gates barred against him
decisions.reason: "The earth" here is the world below, the place of the dead (Exodus 15:12; Psalm 63:10), whose gates are barred (Job 17:16; Psalm 107:16). The gates closed behind Jonah "forever"; he was as good as dead. The words can also mean that the land, with its bars, was shut against him, so that he could not return to it.

decisions.choice: you brought up my life from the pit: God rescued him from death
decisions.reason: "The pit" is another name for the grave or the world of the dead (Psalm 16:10; 30:4, 10). Jonah went down; God brought him up. The rescue has already happened, in the fish.

decisions.choice: the earth with its bars (L); the earth's bars (B); the land of the dead locked me in (R); the pit (L, B); the grave (R)
decisions.reason: Literal and Balanced keep the picture of the earth's bars. Readable says what it means (m2), and "the grave" for the pit, as for Sheol in verse 3. Readable says "brought me up alive" for "brought up my life".

records.source: בְּהִתְעַטֵּ֤ף עָלַי֙ נַפְשִׁ֔י אֶת־יְהוָ֖ה זָכָ֑רְתִּי וַתָּב֤וֹא אֵלֶ֨יךָ֙ תְּפִלָּתִ֔י אֶל־הֵיכַ֖ל קָדְשֶֽׁךָ׃
records.gloss: When fainted on me my life, Yahweh I remembered, and came to you my prayer, to [the] temple of your holiness.
pieces: As my life was ebbing away, \q I remembered {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}, \q and my prayer came to {{deity_pronoun:you|You}}, \q into {{deity_pronoun:your|Your}} holy temple.

L.8: When my life was fainting within me, \q I remembered {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}, \q and my prayer came to {{deity_pronoun:you|You}}, \q to {{deity_pronoun:your|Your}} holy temple.

R.8: When I was about to die, I remembered {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}. \q My prayer reached {{deity_pronoun:you|You}} in {{deity_pronoun:your|Your}} holy temple.

decisions.choice: my life was fainting: my strength was failing, I was close to death
decisions.reason: The verb is used of people fainting from hunger or thirst (Lamentations 2:12, 19; Psalm 107:5). Jonah's life was ebbing away when he turned to the LORD.

decisions.choice: my prayer came to your holy temple: the prayer was heard
decisions.reason: This answers verse 5, where Jonah hoped to look toward the temple again. His prayer reached the LORD where he is present (Psalm 18:7: "he heard my voice from his temple").

decisions.choice: fainting within me (L); ebbing away (B); about to die (R)
decisions.reason: Readable says plainly what the picture means (m1), and joins the four lines into two.

records.gloss: [Those] paying regard to vanities of emptiness their loyal love forsake.
pieces: Those who devote themselves to useless idols \q abandon their loyal love.

L.9: Those who keep empty vanities \q forsake their loyal love.

R.9: People who worship idols that cannot help them \q turn their backs on faithful love.

decisions.choice: those who keep empty vanities: as Psalm 31:7
decisions.reason: Psalm 31:7 says "I hate those who keep empty vanities, but I trust in the LORD". The phrase means worthless idols, things with no reality or power. Jonah, like the psalmist, sets the worshipers of idols against himself (verse 10).

decisions.choice: their loyal love: either the loyalty they owe, or the God who would show them loyal love
alternatives: their source of loyal love, that is, God
decisions.reason: The Hebrew word is *hesed*, loyal love. "Their" loyal love may be the loyalty they should have kept and have given up, or the loyal love that would be theirs, the God who shows it (Psalm 144:2 calls God "my loyal love"). Either way, those who turn to idols lose what is truly faithful.

decisions.choice: those who forsake: said by Jonah, though the pagan sailors have just turned to the LORD
decisions.reason: Jonah speaks of idol worshipers as those who forsake loyal love. The reader has just seen the sailors, who cried to their own gods, turn to the LORD with sacrifice and vows (1:16), while Jonah forsook his calling. The book lets the contrast stand without comment.

decisions.choice: empty vanities (L); useless idols (B); idols that cannot help them (R); loyal love (L, B); faithful love (R)
decisions.reason: Each level reuses the wording of Psalm 31:7 at that level for the idols (m1). *Hesed* is "loyal love" at Literal and Balanced and "faithful love" at Readable, as set for the prophets. Readable says "turn their backs on" for "forsake" and keeps the phrase open, as the Hebrew does (m2).

records.source: וַאֲנִ֗י בְּק֤וֹל תּוֹדָה֙ אֶזְבְּחָה־לָּ֔ךְ אֲשֶׁ֥ר נָדַ֖רְתִּי אֲשַׁלֵּ֑מָה יְשׁוּעָ֖תָה לַיהוָֽה׃ס
records.gloss: And I, with [the] voice of thanksgiving I will sacrifice to you; what I have vowed I will pay. Salvation [belongs] to Yahweh.
pieces: But I will sacrifice to {{deity_pronoun:you|You}} with a song of thanksgiving; \q what I have vowed I will make good. \q It is {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} who saves."

L.10: But I, with the voice of thanksgiving, will sacrifice to {{deity_pronoun:you|You}}; \q what I have vowed I will pay. \q Salvation [belongs] to {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}."

R.10: But I will sing to {{deity_pronoun:you|You}} with thanks and offer {{deity_pronoun:you|You}} a sacrifice. \q I will do what I promised. \q {{divine_name:The LORD|Yahweh}} is the one who saves."

decisions.choice: a sacrifice with thanksgiving, and vows paid: the worship of one rescued
decisions.reason: A person rescued from danger came to the temple to offer a thanksgiving sacrifice, to sing God's praise and to pay the vows made in distress (Leviticus 7:12; Psalm 50:14; 116:17-18). Jonah promises to do what the sailors have already done (1:16).

decisions.choice: salvation belongs to the LORD: as Psalm 3:9
decisions.reason: Psalm 3:9 says "To the LORD belongs salvation". The psalm ends with its summary: rescue is the LORD's to give. It is the last word of Jonah's prayer, and the story goes on to show that the LORD gives it to Nineveh as well (3:10; 4:2).

decisions.choice: But I: Jonah sets himself against the idol worshipers
decisions.reason: The Hebrew puts "I" first, in contrast with those of verse 9.

decisions.choice: with the voice of thanksgiving (L); with a song of thanksgiving (B); sing to you with thanks (R); It is the LORD who saves (B); the one who saves (R)
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable reuse the wording of Psalm 3:9 at their levels for the last line; Literal keeps Jonah's order, salvation first. The "voice of thanksgiving" is a song or shout of praise. Readable says "do what I promised" for paying vows. The double quotation mark closes Jonah's prayer.

records.source: וַיֹּ֥אמֶר יְהוָ֖ה לַדָּ֑ג וַיָּקֵ֥א אֶת־יוֹנָ֖ה אֶל־הַיַּבָּשָֽׁה׃פ
records.gloss: And spoke Yahweh to the fish, and it vomited out Jonah onto the dry land.
pieces: Then {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} spoke to the fish, and it vomited Jonah out onto dry land.

L.11: And {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} spoke to the fish, and it vomited Jonah out onto the dry land.

R.11: Then {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} gave the fish an order, and it threw up Jonah onto dry land.

decisions.choice: the LORD spoke to the fish: the fish obeys at once
decisions.reason: The LORD speaks, and the fish does what he says, as the wind and the sea did (1:4, 15). Jonah, the prophet, is the one creature in the story who would not obey.

decisions.choice: vomited Jonah onto the dry land: an earthy word for the end of the rescue
decisions.reason: The verb is the ordinary word for vomiting (Leviticus 18:25-28; Proverbs 23:8). "The dry land" is the land Jonah named in his confession (1:9) and that the sailors could not reach (1:13).

decisions.choice: vomited ... out (L, B); threw up (R)
decisions.reason: Every level keeps the blunt verb of the Hebrew, in the everyday form at Readable.
